overview: The table presents dense, scannable rows of structured records. It layers class-driven column sizing (--fixed layout with width tiers and a flexing/truncating column) and optional treatments — zebra striping, a pinned first column, and row peeking — on top of a semantic <table>. Wrap it in .uix-table-wrap to get the scroll container and sticky header.
whenToUse: Use a table when users compare records field-by-field across many rows.
Use `fixed` layout with the width-tier classes so columns stay aligned as content changes.
Use `zebra` striping for wide tables where the eye needs help tracking a row across columns.
Use a pinned first column when the identifier must stay visible during horizontal scroll.
do: Give every column a <th scope="col"> so screen readers announce the header with each cell.
Let one content column flex-and-truncate; snap the rest to width tiers rather than hand-coding px.
Keep numeric columns right-aligned and consistent in precision for easy scanning.
Wrap the table in .uix-table-wrap so the header stays sticky and horizontal scroll is contained.
dont: Don't use a table purely for visual layout — it changes the semantics for assistive tech.
Don't omit column headers or use presentational <div>s where <th>/<td> belong.
Don't pack interactive controls into cells without a discernible accessible name.
Don't set fixed pixel widths inline when a width-tier class expresses the same intent.
a11yNotes: Built on a real <table> with <thead>/<tbody> and scoped <th>, so row/column relationships are exposed natively.
The sticky header keeps column context in view while scrolling long tables.
Interactive cell affordances (row actions, pin) carry aria-labels since their glyphs have no text.
Truncated cells keep their full value in the accessible name; visual clipping is not data loss.
